title: OmniStudio Consultant Certification - Practice Exam
description: 60-question timed practice exam mirroring the official blueprint domain weights. 105 minutes, pass with 67% or higher.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Permission Set License and a Permission Set in OmniStudio?
options: They are the same thing with two names.
The Permission Set License determines whether a user is entitled to the feature, while the Permission Set determines what the user can actually do with it.
The Permission Set grants the license automatically.
The Permission Set License is only for admins.
questions.explanation: The Permission Set License determines whether a user is entitled to the licensed feature, while the Permission Set determines what the user can actually do with it, and both are typically required. Option A is wrong because they are distinct layers. Option C is wrong because a Permission Set does not grant the license. Option D is wrong because the Permission Set License is not admin-only.

questions.question: After discovery, the architect has a list of requirements and assumptions. What is the correct way to lock these down before design begins?
options: Keep them in the architect's notes and proceed with design.
Write down the assumptions, confirm them with the customer in writing, and produce a requirements baseline with acceptance criteria that the customer signs off on.
Share them verbally in a meeting and start building.
Wait until after the build to document what was decided.
questions.explanation: Assumptions must be written down and confirmed in writing, and the requirements baseline with acceptance criteria should be signed off before design, because that baseline is what the design is measured against. Option A is wrong because unshared notes do not validate assumptions. Option C is wrong because verbal agreement is not a durable baseline. Option D is wrong because documenting after the build leaves the design unmeasured.

questions.question: A client needs to call an external billing system to fetch pricing, with no user interface involved. Which OmniStudio tool is the right choice?
options: An Integration Procedure.
A FlexCard.
An OmniScript.
A Data Mapper.
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure is the server-side orchestration for calling external systems, which is exactly a system-to-system pricing call with no UI. Option B is wrong because a FlexCard is a UI display component. Option C is wrong because an OmniScript is a user-facing journey. Option D is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data rather than making system calls.

questions.question: A client has three roles that need OmniStudio: builders, reviewers, and end users. How should the architect grant access?
options: Give every user the full builder permission set and license.
Create a small set of role-based permission sets, such as builder, reviewer, and end user, assign each the minimum access it needs, and assign the appropriate license to each role's users.
Create a separate permission set for every individual user.
Give no one any access and rely on the base platform.
questions.explanation: The architect should create a small set of role-based permission sets, assign each the minimum access it needs, and assign the appropriate Permission Set License to each role's users, which is maintainable and least-privilege. Option A is wrong because giving everyone the full builder set over-grants access. Option C is wrong because one-off sets per person are unmaintainable. Option D is wrong because OmniStudio needs the license and permission sets to be usable.

questions.question: A partner plans to build an OmniStudio solution once and install it into many customer orgs. Why does the metadata-based design of OmniStudio support this model?
options: Because OmniStudio artifacts are compiled into a single binary that cannot be reused.
Because every OmniStudio artifact is metadata that can be versioned, deployed through change sets or a DevOps pipeline, and reused across orgs.
Because each customer org must rebuild every artifact from scratch.
Because OmniStudio artifacts are stored only in the customer's browser cache.
questions.explanation: OmniStudio artifacts are metadata, so they can be versioned, deployed through change sets or a DevOps pipeline, and reused across orgs, which is exactly what a build-once-install-many partner model needs. Option A is wrong because there is no single compiled binary. Option C is wrong because reuse across orgs is the point. Option D is wrong because artifacts live in the org's metadata, not the browser cache.

questions.question: A healthcare client needs a patient intake flow that captures sensitive eligibility and benefits data. What is the most important architectural consideration for this use case?
options: Building custom logic that reads all fields regardless of role.
Ensuring the guided flow respects the platform's security model and field-level access so only authorized roles see sensitive data.
Storing all intake data in a single unencrypted custom object.
Avoiding the platform's sharing rules to simplify the flow.
questions.explanation: Healthcare intake involves sensitive data, so the architect must ensure the flow respects the platform's security model and field-level access. Option A is wrong because bypassing field-level access is a privacy violation. Option C is wrong because it ignores data protection. Option D is wrong because sharing rules are part of the correct access model, not something to avoid.

questions.question: An architect has selected a tool for a requirement, but the tool cannot satisfy the acceptance criteria in the requirements baseline. What should the architect do?
options: Force the tool to fit anyway and proceed.
Re-evaluate the tool choice against the baseline and select one that satisfies the criteria.
Change the acceptance criteria to match the tool.
Skip the requirement entirely.
questions.explanation: The selected tool must satisfy the acceptance criteria, data inputs and outputs, and constraints, so if it cannot, the architect re-evaluates the choice rather than forcing the fit. Option A is wrong because forcing a tool that cannot meet the criteria produces a failed design. Option C is wrong because changing the criteria to match the tool hides the problem. Option D is wrong because skipping the requirement does not solve it.

questions.question: A client needs to display a compact account summary on a record page with no user input. Which OmniStudio tool is the right choice?
options: An OmniScript.
A FlexCard.
An Integration Procedure.
A Data Mapper.
questions.explanation: A FlexCard is the reusable, data-driven UI component for displaying a record or set of records, which is exactly the display-only need here. Option A is wrong because an OmniScript is for guided multi-step capture, not display. Option C is wrong because an Integration Procedure is a server-side orchestration with no UI. Option D is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data rather than displaying it.

questions.question: A telecom client needs a guided flow where a rep selects a plan, adds devices and add-ons, and hands off to a quote. Which OmniStudio pattern best fits this process?
options: A single FlexCard that displays the final quote only.
An OmniScript that drives the guided plan, add-on, and eligibility steps, with Integration Procedures pulling pricing and eligibility from the billing system.
A Data Mapper used alone to transform the quote payload.
A custom Apex page that bypasses OmniStudio entirely.
questions.explanation: A telco quote-to-order journey is a guided multi-step process, which is exactly what an OmniScript drives, and the pricing and eligibility lookups belong in Integration Procedures. Option A is wrong because a FlexCard alone cannot drive the guided steps. Option C is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data but does not guide a journey. Option D is wrong because it abandons the declarative value OmniStudio provides for this common pattern.

questions.question: A public-sector client needs a permit application flow that must be auditable. Which approach best supports the auditability requirement?
options: Capturing the submission in a record with a clear audit trail of who submitted what and when.
Storing submissions only in the browser cache.
Allowing any user to edit any submission after it is filed.
Deleting submission history after 30 days to reduce storage.
questions.explanation: Public-sector permit flows need an audit trail, so the architect should capture the submission in a record with clear metadata about who submitted what and when. Option B is wrong because browser cache is not durable or auditable. Option C is wrong because post-filing edits undermine the audit trail. Option D is wrong because deleting history destroys the auditability the process requires.

questions.question: A user clicks a button on a FlexCard and must complete a multi-step guided process to resolve a case. Which action type should be used?
options: A link to a URL
A modal with a small form
Launching an OmniScript
A static text element
questions.explanation: A multi-step guided process is exactly what an OmniScript is for, so the action should launch the OmniScript and pass the context record. A link navigates away without the guided flow, a modal is for a short in-context interaction, and a text element is not an action.

questions.question: A consultant is choosing a data source for a card that only ever shows fixed option labels that never change. What is the correct choice and why?
options: Turbo Extract, because it is the fastest live source
Static JSON, because the data never changes and needs no server round trip
Integration Procedure, because it is the most flexible
Standard Extract, because it can run multiple queries
questions.explanation: Static JSON is embedded in the card definition and needs no server round trip, which is ideal for fixed labels and option lists that never change. Turbo Extract, standard Extract, and Integration Procedure all fetch live data, which is unnecessary and adds latency for data that is constant.

questions.question: A FlexCard must display a flat list of the five most recent cases for the current account, refreshing whenever the record changes. Which data source is the most efficient choice?
options: Static JSON
Turbo Extract
Standard Extract
Integration Procedure
questions.explanation: A Turbo Extract runs a single SOQL query against the context record and returns a flat result set, which is exactly the shape and refresh behavior this card needs, and it is the fastest live-data path. Static JSON cannot reflect live record data. A standard Extract or Integration Procedure adds orchestration the card does not need for a single flat list.

questions.question: A user needs to enter a single short value without leaving the current card. Which action is the best fit?
options: A link to a record page
A modal that opens in context
Launching a full OmniScript
Calling an Integration Procedure with no UI
questions.explanation: A short, focused capture that should not interrupt the user's flow is best handled by a modal that opens in context. A link navigates away, a full OmniScript is overkill for one value, and an IP with no UI gives the user no way to enter the value.

questions.question: Which element is the correct choice for showing a collection of related records on a FlexCard?
options: A text element
A data table
A single input
A menu
questions.explanation: A collection of related records is tabular data, so a data table is the correct element. A text element shows a single value, an input captures one value, and a menu selects from discrete options; none of them present a collection clearly.

questions.question: A FlexCard should show a warning banner only when a case is past its due date. What is the correct implementation?
options: Always show the banner
Add a condition that shows the banner when the due date is past
Hide the banner with a static setting
Remove the banner element
questions.explanation: A condition that evaluates the due date and shows the banner only when it is past is the correct use of conditional rendering. Always showing it ignores the data, a static hide removes it entirely, and removing the element defeats the purpose.

questions.question: A consultant wants to build a reusable detail view that can be embedded in several parent cards. What is the correct design approach?
options: Build the detail into each parent card separately
Create a child FlexCard with an explicit, self-contained data contract that receives its context from the parent
Nest the child five levels deep
Give the child a hard-coded record
questions.explanation: A reusable child FlexCard should have an explicit, self-contained data contract and receive its context from the parent, so it can be embedded in multiple parents. Duplicating the detail in each parent defeats reuse, deep nesting multiplies fetches, and a hard-coded record makes the child unusable elsewhere.

questions.question: What is the correct distinction between data and state in a FlexCard?
options: Data reflects the record; state reflects the user's current interaction
Data reflects the interaction; state reflects the record
They are the same thing
State is stored in the data source
questions.explanation: Data comes from the source and reflects the record, while state reflects the user's current interaction with the card. Confusing them leads to writing interaction state back to the source or failing to update on interaction. They are not the same, and state is not stored in the data source.

questions.question: A FlexCard displays three fields, but its data source returns a wide record with dozens of fields. What best practice is violated?
options: The theme is wrong
The data source is not lean, adding payload and render cost
The card has too few elements
The output variables are not mapped
questions.explanation: A best practice is to return only the fields the card uses, because extra fields add payload and render cost. The theme, element count, and output variables are not the issue; the data source is over-fetching.

questions.question: A card shows cross-record aggregate data for managers. What is the best placement?
options: A Lightning component on a single record page
A tab that gives the card its own space
A console view for agents
A card bound to a case record
questions.explanation: Cross-record aggregate data is not anchored to one record, so a tab placement that gives the card its own space is best. A record-page component or a case-bound card would anchor it to a single record, and a console view is for task-driven agent work, not a manager's aggregate view.

questions.question: A card for a sales rep shows every opportunity field and every possible action. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The data source is too small
The card lacks a chart
The card buries the data and actions that matter under noise
The card is read-only
questions.explanation: Showing every field and action buries the data and actions that matter, forcing the rep to filter mentally. The problem is not the source size, the absence of a chart, or read-only status; it is the lack of role-based focus and clarity.

questions.question: An OmniScript has a 'business or consumer' choice in the first Step. The rest of the flow differs entirely between the two. What is the cleanest branching design?
options: Make every later Element conditional on the choice, one condition each
Make the two divergent phases conditional Steps, each gated on the choice value
Duplicate the whole OmniScript into two versions
Use a Data Mapper to decide the path
questions.explanation: When an entire phase differs, a conditional Step is the right granularity: one condition hides or shows the whole Step. Making every Element conditional creates many hard-to-maintain conditions, duplicating the OmniScript doubles maintenance, and a Data Mapper does not control UI branching.

questions.question: An OmniScript must collect a list of line items, each with a product, quantity, and price. What is the correct element structure?
options: A single Step with one text Input for the whole list
A repeatable Block containing product, quantity, and price Inputs
Three separate Steps, one per field
A read-only Input
questions.explanation: A list of line items is a repeating group, so a repeatable Block is the right structure: each instance holds product, quantity, and price, and writes to its own data JSON node. A single text input cannot hold structured line items, separate Steps fragment the task, and a read-only input cannot capture data.

questions.question: An OmniScript must fetch data from an external REST service, transform the response, and merge it with Salesforce data before showing it to the user. What is the appropriate tool?
options: A Data Mapper
An Integration Procedure that orchestrates the REST call, transform, and merge
A formula Element
A validation rule
questions.explanation: This is multi-step orchestration spanning an external system and Salesforce, which is an Integration Procedure's job. A Data Mapper only transforms one structure to another, a formula computes a value, and a validation rule checks input.

questions.question: A consultant wants the OmniScript to display in Spanish for users whose locale is set to Spanish. Where is the language selection handled?
options: In the OmniScript's global settings, one language for the whole script
Per Element, with the runtime picking the language from the user's locale or a data JSON value
In the Data Mapper that saves the results
In the Integration Procedure that fetches the account
questions.explanation: Multi-language support is configured per Element, and the runtime selects the language from the user's locale or a language value in the data JSON. There is no single global language switch for the whole script, and Data Mappers and Integration Procedures do not control display language.

questions.question: A consultant adds a new branch for a rarely used customer type. What must be done for multi-language support?
options: Nothing, translations are inherited from the parent Step
Add a translation for every Element on the new branch for every supported locale
Add one translation for the whole branch
Set the branch to English only
questions.explanation: Multi-language support is per Element, so every Element on the new branch needs a translation for every supported locale. There is no branch-level translation and no inheritance that covers new Elements.

questions.question: A consultant is deciding whether to build a custom LWC or use a standard element for a simple picklist. What is the better choice?
options: Build the custom LWC for more control
Use the standard picklist, since it already solves the interaction with less cost
Use a FlexCard
Use a Formula
questions.explanation: Standard components should be the default because they cover most needs with less build, test, and maintenance cost. A custom LWC is warranted only when a standard element cannot do the job. A FlexCard is display, and a Formula computes a value.

questions.question: A consultant finishes a walkthrough but has not written any test cases. What is the problem?
options: No problem, the design is complete
A design that cannot be tested is a sketch, not a design; turn it into a test matrix and validate it
Test cases are written by the user
Test cases are optional
questions.explanation: The value of a walkthrough is that it is testable. A design without test cases cannot be validated, so it is a sketch. The walkthrough should end with the test matrix that proves the journey works.

questions.question: A fetch stage in an OmniScript can fail when the external service is down. What is the correct design for this failure?
options: Let it fail silently and continue
Read the returned status and route the failure to a user-facing message or a log
Retry forever until it succeeds
Skip the fetch and use empty data
questions.explanation: Error handling belongs in the flow: the fetch should return a status the OmniScript reads, and failures should surface to the user or a log. Failing silently hides the problem, retrying forever blocks the user, and using empty data produces wrong results.

questions.question: An address capture sub-journey is used in three different parent OmniScripts. What is the appropriate design?
options: Duplicate the address Steps in each parent
Build the address capture once as a child OmniScript and invoke it from each parent
Use a FlexCard for the address
Use a Formula
questions.explanation: When the same sub-journey is reused by multiple parents, build it once as a child OmniScript and invoke it from each, which reduces duplication and keeps behavior consistent. Duplicating the Steps in each parent is the maintenance burden the child avoids, and a FlexCard or Formula does not capture the address.

questions.question: A consultant adds a new branch to an OmniScript that captures a 'preferred contact time' field. The save uses a Data Mapper. What must the consultant do?
options: Nothing, the Data Mapper handles all fields automatically
Update the Data Mapper's save mapping to include the new field
Add a new Integration Procedure
Remove the branch
questions.explanation: The save mapping must include every field captured on every branch, or the new field is silently dropped. A Data Mapper does not automatically pick up new fields, and adding an IP or removing the branch does not address the missing mapping.

questions.question: An external response returns nested JSON that the client component cannot read. What is the strategic approach?
options: Use Set Values to copy the nested fields
Use a Data Mapper Transform to flatten and rename the fields into the output structure
Send the raw JSON to the client
Change the HTTP method
questions.explanation: The Data Mapper Transform is built to reshape data, including flattening nested structures and renaming fields. Set Values assigns values and is not suited to structural reshaping. Sending raw JSON or changing the method does not fix the structure.

questions.question: A consultant maps a nested JSON response directly into flat output variables and the client component shows empty fields. What is the correct fix?
options: Change the HTTP method
Add a Data Mapper Transform action to reshape the response
Increase the timeout
Switch to basic authentication
questions.explanation: Nested JSON needs reshaping before it fits flat output variables, and the Data Mapper Transform action is the tool for that. The HTTP method, timeout, and auth protocol do not affect how the response is structured.

questions.question: A customer needs to read a single account record from an external REST API by its ID. Which HTTP method and request surface should the consultant use?
options: POST with the ID in the body
GET with the ID in the resource path or query parameter
DELETE with the ID in the body
PUT with the ID in the header
questions.explanation: Reading a resource is a GET, and the record identifier belongs in the resource path or a query parameter. POST creates, DELETE removes, and PUT updates, so none of those fit a read operation.

questions.question: Where is the authentication protocol for an external call configured in an Integration Procedure?
options: Inside the HTTP Action's request body
In the named credential referenced by the HTTP Action
In the Data Mapper Transform action
In the IP's output variables
questions.explanation: Authentication is held by the named credential, which the HTTP Action references. The request body carries data, not auth configuration. The Data Mapper and output variables handle data transformation, not connection security.

questions.question: Where should the final reshaping of data happen in an Integration Procedure?
options: Inside the Response action
In the Data Mapper Transform and Set Values actions before the Response action
In the named credential
In the HTTP Action's request body
questions.explanation: Reshaping and value assignment belong in the Data Mapper Transform and Set Values actions that run before the Response action. The Response action should only assemble the already-shaped data. The named credential and request body are not for response shaping.

questions.question: Where should external endpoint URLs and secrets be stored for an Integration Procedure?
options: In the IP's output variables
In named credentials referenced by the HTTP Actions
In a custom label
In the Data Mapper Transform action
questions.explanation: Named credentials are the security boundary that holds endpoints and secrets, and the HTTP Actions reference them. Output variables, custom labels, and the Data Mapper are not the place for connection details or secrets.

questions.question: A customer's legacy system exposes only a SOAP API. How should the consultant configure the HTTP Action?
options: Use GET with a JSON body
Use POST with an XML SOAP envelope as the request body
Use DELETE with the operation in the header
Use PUT with a form-encoded body
questions.explanation: SOAP calls are POST requests whose body is an XML envelope containing the operation and parameters. GET, DELETE, and PUT do not match the SOAP contract, and the body must be XML, not JSON or form-encoded.

questions.question: Why should a consultant avoid automatically retrying a POST operation on timeout?
options: Retries are always faster
The first call may have succeeded, so a retry can create a duplicate record
POST operations never time out
Retries are not supported
questions.explanation: A POST is non-idempotent, so if the first call succeeded but the response was lost, a retry creates a duplicate record. Retries must be considered per operation, and non-idempotent calls need special handling.

questions.question: In a read scenario, the client needs a filtered list from a REST endpoint. Where should the filter be applied for best performance?
options: In the client component after the data arrives
In the request query parameters so the endpoint returns only matching records
In the Response action
In the named credential
questions.explanation: Filtering in the request query parameters lets the endpoint return only the matching records, minimizing payload and latency. Filtering in the client wastes bandwidth, and the Response action and named credential are not for filtering.

questions.question: A consultant is configuring an HTTP Action and wants the external endpoint URL to be changeable without editing the IP. What is the correct approach?
options: Hard-code the URL in the HTTP Action
Store the URL in a named credential and reference it from the HTTP Action
Put the URL in a custom label and reference it in the request body
Set the URL as a static resource
questions.explanation: The named credential is the single place where the endpoint URL and authentication live, so changing the endpoint means editing the credential, not the IP. Hard-coding the URL forces edits in every IP. Custom labels and static resources are not the mechanism for endpoint configuration.

questions.question: A source sends a date in one format and the target requires another. How should the mapping handle it?
options: Pass the date through unchanged
Use a date function to convert the format
Reject the record
Store the raw string
questions.explanation: A date function converts the format to what the target expects. Passing it through keeps the wrong format, and rejecting or storing raw does not convert it.

questions.question: A consultant needs to read data across related objects. Which Data Mapper type supports the relationship traversal?
options: Turbo Extract
Extract
Load
Transform
questions.explanation: Extract supports the full SOQL feature set including relationship traversal. Turbo Extract has a narrower feature set, Load writes, and Transform does not query.

questions.question: A flow reads a large dataset but only a subset is needed. What best practice should the consultant apply to the read step?
options: Read all records and filter later
Filter in the query to read only what is needed
Use a Load to read
Map every field
questions.explanation: Filtering in the query reads only the needed records, keeping the read light. Reading all and filtering later wastes resources, and the other options do not reduce the read.

questions.question: A Load must update existing records and the incoming data does not carry the Salesforce record ID. What must the consultant do?
options: Insert the records as new
Resolve the target record through a lookup
Skip the update
Use a Transform instead
questions.explanation: An update must resolve the target record, and a lookup does that when the ID is absent. Inserting creates duplicates, skipping loses the update, and a Transform does not write.

questions.question: A consultant needs to read records that span multiple related objects using relationship traversal. Which Data Mapper type should be chosen?
options: Turbo Extract
Load
Extract
Transform
questions.explanation: Extract supports the full SOQL feature set including relationship traversal. Turbo Extract has a narrower feature set, Load writes, and Transform does not query Salesforce.

questions.question: A consultant is mapping data where a source field must be renamed and its value transformed before it lands in the target. What is the correct approach?
options: Copy the field directly by name
Map the field explicitly and apply the needed transformation
Skip the field and let the target default
Read the field in a separate Data Mapper
questions.explanation: Complex mapping requires an explicit field mapping with the transformation applied. A direct copy ignores the transformation, and skipping or splitting the field does not produce the correct value.

questions.question: A Data Mapper reads a large dataset but only a few records are needed. What is the most effective performance optimization?
options: Filter in the SOQL WHERE clause
Filter in the output mapping
Read all records and discard extras
Use a Load instead of an Extract
questions.explanation: Filtering in the WHERE clause reduces the data read at the database. Output filtering still pulls the full dataset, and the other options do not reduce the read.

questions.question: A flow reads source data, reshapes it, and writes it to Salesforce. What is the correct sequence of Data Mapper types?
options: Load, Transform, Extract
Extract or Turbo Extract, Transform, Load
Transform, Load, Extract
Load, Extract, Transform
questions.explanation: The flow reads with Extract or Turbo Extract, reshapes with Transform, and writes with Load. The other orders do not match the read, reshape, write sequence.

questions.question: Two Data Mappers in a flow read the same records. What is the best performance improvement?
options: Keep both reads
Reuse the data from the first read instead of re-querying
Add more fields to both
Use a Transform between them
questions.explanation: Reusing data already in context eliminates the duplicate read. Keeping both reads wastes resources, and the other options do not remove the redundancy.

questions.question: A Data Mapper reads a large dataset but only a subset of records is needed. Where should the filter be applied for best results?
options: In the output mapping only
In the SOQL WHERE clause of the query
In the target object definition
In a separate Transform after the read
questions.explanation: Filtering in the WHERE clause reduces the data read at the source. Output filtering still pulls the full dataset, and the other options do not filter the read.

questions.question: In which model does the architect decide whether an address is its own entity or part of an account?
options: Conceptual Model
Logical Model
Physical Model
None, it is a business decision only
questions.explanation: The Logical Model is where the data structure is decided, including whether an address is its own entity or part of an account. The Conceptual Model stays in business language without that structure. The Physical Model implements the decision already made. It is a data-structure decision, not only a business one.

questions.question: An architect is designing for a solution that will grow from hundreds to millions of records. Which practice best supports scalability?
options: Return full result sets so no data is ever missing
Keep queries selective and bounded, and cache read-mostly reference data
Run all work synchronously so results are always current
Store all external data in custom settings
questions.explanation: Selective and bounded queries plus cached reference data keep the solution within limits as data grows. Returning full result sets will hit row limits at scale. Running all work synchronously blocks users and does not scale. Custom settings are for configuration, not for storing large external datasets.

questions.question: A team is about to edit an OmniScript directly in production to fix a quick issue. What is the correct governance response?
options: Allow it because it is fast and declarative
Reject it and require the change to go through a sandbox and a deployment gate
Allow it but log the change manually
Allow it only for Integration Procedures
questions.explanation: Direct production edits bypass review, testing, and rollback, so the correct response is to reject it and require the change to flow through a sandbox and a deployment gate. Allowing it, even with manual logging, still lacks the controlled process. Restricting the exception to Integration Procedures does not address the risk for OmniScripts.

questions.question: A Data Raptor that filters on a non-indexed field is slow and returns thousands of rows. What is the correct fix?
options: Remove the filter so the query returns everything
Filter on an indexed field and add a row limit where the business allows
Run the query inside a loop to split the work
Convert the Data Raptor to a FlexCard
questions.explanation: Filtering on an indexed field makes the query selective, and a row limit bounds the result set, which addresses both the slowness and the row-count risk. Removing the filter returns even more rows. Running the query in a loop multiplies the queries and hits limits. A FlexCard is a display component and does not fix the query.

questions.question: An OmniScript must save a parent record and several child records that must all succeed together. What is the best approach?
options: A save Data Raptor that writes the parent only
An Integration Procedure that orchestrates the multi-record save with error handling
A separate Data Raptor for each record with no coordination
A FlexCard that submits the records
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure can orchestrate the multi-record save and handle errors so a partial write does not leave the data inconsistent. A Data Raptor writing only the parent loses the children. Separate uncoordinated Data Raptors risk partial writes. A FlexCard is a display component and does not orchestrate saves.

questions.question: An architect is choosing between a lookup and a master-detail relationship for related records. What should drive the decision?
options: The default, which is always master-detail
The cascade, sharing, and reporting needs of the relationship
The number of fields on the object
The name of the object
questions.explanation: The choice between lookup and master-detail should be driven by the cascade, sharing, and reporting needs, because master-detail cascades deletes and controls access while a lookup is more flexible. The default is not always master-detail. Field count and object name do not determine the relationship type.

questions.question: A complex transformation must produce identical results for three OmniScripts. Where should it live?
options: Duplicated inside each OmniScript
In a single shared Integration Procedure
In the browser's JavaScript for each script
In a custom label that stores the output
questions.explanation: A single shared Integration Procedure guarantees identical results and is written and tested once. Duplicating it in each script risks drift. Browser JavaScript duplicated per script has the same drift problem. A custom label stores text, not a transformation result.

questions.question: A solution needs a read-only summary of a customer's open cases displayed on the account record page. The data is already in Salesforce. What is the best fit?
options: An OmniScript that queries the cases on load
An Integration Procedure called from a custom component
A FlexCard with a Data Raptor that reads the cases
A scheduled Apex job that writes the summary to a field
questions.explanation: A FlexCard is designed for embedded, read-only display and a Data Raptor reads the cases directly from Salesforce, which is the lightest correct fit. An OmniScript is overkill for a display-only widget. An Integration Procedure adds a server round trip for data that is already local. A scheduled job introduces staleness and extra writes for a read-only need.

questions.question: An architect is defining the test plan for a new Integration Procedure that writes to an external system. What must the plan cover?
options: Only the happy path
External calls, payloads, and failure handling, plus the security context
Only the build, since it is declarative
Only the OmniScript that calls it
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure that writes externally must be tested for its external calls, payloads, and failure handling, and for its security context, because those are where it can fail or expose data. Testing only the happy path misses the error cases. Testing only the build ignores behavior. Testing only the calling OmniScript ignores the IP's own behavior.
